2005B16.goal: $x^2+mx+n=0$ has roots twice those of $x^2+px+m=0$. We want $\tfrac np$. Use Vieta on both.
2005B16.approach: Let the small roots be $r,s$: $r+s=-p$, $rs=m$. Then $-m=2(r+s)=-2p$ and $n=4rs=4m$. So $m=2p$, $n=8p$.

check.q: If the roots double, how does their sum change?
If the roots double, how does their product change?

2005B16.shortcut: Check with $p=1$: $x^2+x+2$ and $x^2+2x+8$; the second's roots are double the first's.
traps: Doubling the product instead of quadrupling.
2005B16.recognize: Roots scaled by $k$: sum scales by $k$, product by $k^2$.

tools.name: Chaining powers
tools.why: Substitute each equation into the next.

2005B17.bridge: Substitute each equation into the next to get $4^{abcd}=8$.
2005B17.recognize: Chains of exponential equations: substitute to telescope.

2005B18.goal: Phone numbers $555$-$abc$-$defg$ with $a<b<\cdots<g$, distinct digits from $2$–$9$. Count them. Increasing order means choosing a set is enough.

tools.name: Increasing sequences
tools.fact: \text{a set of digits gives exactly one increasing arrangement}

2005B18.approach: $\binom87=8$: choose which one of $2$–$9$ to leave out.
2005B18.bridge: Increasing order turns this into choosing a subset.
solution: Each choice gives one increasing order.
2005B18.recognize: Strictly increasing digit strings: combinations, not permutations.

2005B19.goal: Score distribution: $10\%$ got $70$, $25\%$ got $80$, $20\%$ got $85$, $15\%$ got $90$, $30\%$ got $95$. We want $|\text{mean}-\text{median}|$.
2005B19.approach: Cumulative: $10,35,55,\ldots$ — the $50\%$ mark lies in the $85$ group, so the median is $85$. Mean $=7+20+17+13.5+28.5=86$.
2005B19.bridge: Cumulative percents for the median; weights for the mean.
2005B19.shortcut: Use $20$ students: $2,5,4,3,6$ of each score — the 10th and 11th are both $85$.
traps: Taking the median as the middle listed score ($85$ coincidentally, but for the wrong reason).
2005B19.recognize: Median from a frequency table: find where the cumulative share crosses $50\%$.

2005B20.goal: Average all $5!=120$ numbers made from $1,3,5,7,8$. By symmetry each digit appears equally often in each place.

tools.name: Positional symmetry
tools.fact: \text{each digit is in each place }24\text{ times}

traps: Averaging only the largest and smallest numbers.
2005B20.recognize: Sums or averages over all digit permutations: positional symmetry.

2005B21.goal: $40$ slips, numbers $1$–$10$ four times each; draw $4$. $p=P(\text{all same})$, $q=P(\text{two pairs})$. We want $\tfrac qp$; the common denominator $\binom{40}4$ cancels.

tools.name: Favourable counts
tools.why: Choose the numbers, then the slips.

steps.title: Counts
steps.explain: All four the same: $10$ ways. Two pairs: $\binom{10}2=45$ number choices, $\binom42=6$ slip choices for each.

2005B21.bridge: Compare favourable counts; the total cancels.
2005B21.shortcut: Ordering $a,b$ would double-count: $90\cdot36/10=324$ is the trap.
traps: Using $10\cdot9$ for the pair of numbers (ordered).
2005B21.recognize: Ratio of probabilities with the same sample space: ratio of counts.

2005B22.goal: For $n\le24$, when does $\tfrac{n(n+1)}2$ divide $n!$? Simplify to whether $n+1$ divides $2(n-1)!$.

tools.name: Primes block divisibility
tools.why: All factors of $(n-1)!$ are smaller than $n+1$.

2005B22.approach: It fails exactly when $n+1$ is an odd prime: $3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$ — $8$ values. Composite $n+1$ (and $n+1=2$) work. Answer $24-8=16$.

steps.title: Failure condition
steps.explain: If $n+1=p$ is an odd prime, $p$ divides neither $2$ nor $(n-1)!$. If $n+1$ is composite, its factors appear in $2(n-1)!$.

check.q: How many odd primes are at most $25$?

2005B22.bridge: Reduce to whether $n+1$ is an odd prime.
solution: Fails iff $n+1$ is an odd prime: $8$ values.
traps: Counting primes up to $24$ instead of $25$.
2005B22.recognize: Factorials divisible by an expression: primes larger than every factor block it.

2005B23.goal: Trapezoid $AB\parallel DC$; $EF$ joins the midpoints of the legs. $[ABEF]=2[FECD]$. We want $\tfrac{AB}{DC}$. The midline cuts the height in half and has length $\tfrac{AB+DC}2$.

tools.name: Midline
tools.why: The segment joining leg midpoints is the average of the bases.

check.q: What is the length of the midline of a trapezoid with bases $a,b$?

2005B23.bridge: Use the midline length and equal heights.
traps: Treating the pieces' areas as proportional to $AB$ and $DC$ alone.
2005B23.recognize: Trapezoid cut by its midline: both halves have the same height.

2005B24.goal: $x=\overline{ab}$, $y=\overline{ba}$ with $x^2-y^2=m^2$. We want $x+y+m$. Factor the difference of squares.

tools.name: Square condition
tools.why: $11$ must appear an even number of times.

2005B24.approach: $a+b=11$, so $m^2=9\cdot121(a-b)$, needing $a-b$ a square. $a-b$ is odd (since $a+b$ is odd) and less than $9$: $a-b=1$. So $x=65$, $y=56$, $m=33$.
2005B24.bridge: $11\mid a+b$, then make $a-b$ a perfect square.
2005B24.recognize: Reversed digits: $x\pm y$ factor as $9(a-b)$ and $11(a+b)$.

2005B25.goal: Choose the largest $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,100\}$ with no two elements summing to $125$. Pair up numbers that sum to $125$.

tools.name: Pairing
tools.why: $38$ pairs; at most one from each.

tools.name: Free numbers
tools.why: Their partners ($101$–$124$) aren't in the set.

2005B25.approach: Take all of $1$–$24$ ($24$) plus one from each of the $38$ pairs: $62$.

steps.title: Maximum
steps.explain: $24+38=62$, and no set can do better (at most one per pair).

2005B25.bridge: Free numbers plus one from each pair.
solution: $1$–$24$ have no partner in range: all allowed.
2005B25.recognize: "No two sum to $S$": pair complements; free elements are added in full.
